name: Executive Order of April 12, 1870 (establishing the Fort Berthold Reservation)
promises: This was an executive order, not a treaty. President Grant set apart a reservation for the three nations, which had held their territory under the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty and by aboriginal title north and east of the Missouri.
An unratified agreement made at Fort Berthold on July 27, 1866 had preceded it; the Senate never ratified that agreement (Docket 350-B).

breaches.what: The nations claimed for the lands lost under the 1870 and 1880 executive orders that drew their reservation boundaries (Docket 350-D). After a trial on value the claim was settled for $3,200,000 by compromise, without a finding.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Dockets 350-C and 350-D, 37 Ind. Cl. Comm. 502 (1976)

source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

breaches.what: The MHA Nation says the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty recognised over 12 million acres as its homeland and that later treaties, executive orders and Acts of Congress reduced this to less than 3 million.
breaches.whoFoundIt: MHA Nation (Three Affiliated Tribes), History page

compensation: No payment at the time. Compromise judgments of $3,200,000 (Docket 350-D, the 1870 and 1880 boundary orders) and $6,500,000 (Docket 350-C, aboriginal lands) in 1976.
today: In 1971 the Indian Claims Commission first held that this order extinguished the nations' aboriginal title north and east of the Missouri, but in 1975 it called that holding erroneous: the nations kept using the land, did not accept the 1870 reservation in exchange for their claims, and their title ended only when Congress acted in the Act of March 3, 1891, effective May 20, 1891 (35 Ind. Cl. Comm. 269). That aboriginal-land claim (Docket 350-C) was settled for $6,500,000 in 1976.

nationVoice.summary: Counts the executive orders and federal acts after 1851 as the steps by which over 12 million recognised acres became less than 3 million.

openQuestions: The order's text (1 Kappler 883) was not opened; textUrl points to the ICC opinion that discusses it.

No finding was made that this order itself took land in breach of the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty; the ICC's 1975 view is that the order did not extinguish the nations' title at all. A finding on what the order removed from the Fort Laramie territory would change the status.
Royce's areas 529, 620 and 621 under this id were not each matched to a docket.

plain.promised: This was an executive order, not a treaty. President Grant set apart a reservation for the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara, who held their territory under the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty and by aboriginal title.
plain.happened: The MHA Nation says executive orders and acts of Congress cut its over 12 million recognised acres to less than 3 million. The claim over this order was settled without a finding; no formal finding of breach has been located.
plain.today: Compromise judgments of $3,200,000 for the 1870 and 1880 boundary orders and $6,500,000 for aboriginal lands were entered in 1976. Whether they were paid has not been traced.
